content: The pound, also known as the pound-mass (abbreviation: lb, or sometimes in the United States), is a unit of mass used in the imperial, United States customary, and other measurement systems. One pound is equivalent to 453.59237 grams. The term pound originates from the Latin word pendere, meaning to weigh. The Latin word libra, which means scales or balances, also referred to a Roman unit of mass similar to the pound. This is the origin of the abbreviation lb for the pound. Historically, the pound has been defined differently across various regions, time periods, and applications, leading to broadly similar but not identical standards of mass or weight. English Pounds In England, several definitions of the pound have been used, including the avoirdupois pound, the Troy pound, the Tower pound, the merchant's pound, and the London pound. There is a historical connection between the pound as a unit of mass and the pound as a unit of currency. Originally, the pound sterling was equivalent to the value of a Tower pound of silver, which would be worth approximately £79 or $158 USD today. In 1528, the standard was changed to the Troy pound, worth about £84 or $168 USD today. Avoirdupois Pound The avoirdupois pound was introduced by London merchants in 1303. Initially, it was based on independent standards measured to be approximately 7,002 troy grains. During the reign of Henry VIII, the avoirdupois pound was redefined as exactly 7,000 troy grains. Since then, the grain has often been considered part of the avoirdupois system. One kilogram is equivalent to approximately 2.20462278 pounds. This value was determined using independently maintained artifacts that served as the official standard for this pound. This older value is sometimes referred to as the imperial pound, though this terminology is now obsolete unless referring to the slightly different 1878 definition. In the United States, the avoirdupois pound has been officially defined in terms of the kilogram since 1893, with one kilogram equaling approximately 2.20462 pounds. The current international pound differs from the U.S. 1894 pound by about one part in 10 million. In 1958, the United States and Commonwealth countries agreed on common definitions for the pound and the yard. In the United Kingdom, the international pound was implemented through the Weights and Measures Act of 1963. An avoirdupois pound is equal to 16 avoirdupois ounces or exactly 7,000 grains. Troy Pound The Troy pound derives its name from the French market town of Troyes, where English merchants traded as early as the time of Charlemagne (early 9th century). The Troy weight system was used in England by apothecaries and jewelers. A Troy pound is equal to 12 Troy ounces or 5,760 grains, which is approximately 373.241721 grams. The Troy pound is no longer in general use. In Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom, and other regions, the Troy pound is no longer a legal unit for trade. In the United Kingdom, its use was abolished on January 6, 1879. However, the Troy ounce is still used for measuring precious metals such as gold, silver, and platinum, as well as some gemstones like opals. Most measurements of precious metals in pounds refer to Troy pounds, even if not explicitly stated. Tower Pound The Tower pound was based on the wheat grain, unlike other English measures, which were based on the barley grain. Merchant's Pound The merchant's pound (also known as the mercantile pound, libra mercantoria, or commercial pound) was equal to 9,600 wheat grains (15 Tower ounces or 6,750 grains). It was used in England until the 14th century for most goods, excluding money, spices, and electuaries. London Pound The London pound was equal to 7,200 troy grains (16 Tower ounces or 15 Troy ounces). Wool Pound The wool pound was equal to 6,992 grains and was used as a unit of mass to measure the quantity of wool. Roman Libra The libra (Latin for pound) was an ancient Roman unit of mass equivalent to approximately 327 grams. It was divided into 12 unciae, or ounces. The libra is the origin of the abbreviation lb for the pound. French Livre Since the Middle Ages, various pounds have been used in France. The word pound translates to livre in French, a term still used today to refer to a metric pound. The livre métrique was set equal to the kilogram by decree between 1800 and 1812, serving as an official metric pound. The livre usuelle was set equal to 500 grams by decree in 1812 but was abolished as a unit of mass effective January 1, 1840. Russian Funt The Russian pound (фунт, funt) was an obsolete Russian unit of mass equivalent to approximately 409.5124 grams. Jersey Pound The Jersey pound was an obsolete unit of mass used on the island of Jersey from the 14th to the 19th century. It was equivalent to about 7,561 grains and may have been derived from the French livre poids de marc. Trone Pound The trone pound was one of several obsolete Scottish units of measurement. It was equivalent to between 21 and 28 avoirdupois ounces. Metric Pounds In many countries, with the introduction of the metric system, the pound (or its translation) became an informal term for half a kilogram or 500 grams, often following an official redefinition of an existing unit during the 19th century. The Dutch pond is an exception, as it was officially redefined as 1 kilogram, with an ounce of 100 grams. Today, in the Netherlands, the term pond likely refers to 500 grams, while the former definition is no longer used. However, the 100-gram ounce remains in limited use. In daily life, pond is exclusively used for amounts of 500 grams, as is ons for 100 grams. In German, the term is Pfund, in French livre, in Dutch pond, in Spanish and Portuguese libra, and in Italian libbra. Hundreds of older pounds were replaced in this way. Although the pound persists as an informal term in these countries to varying degrees, scales and measuring devices are denominated only in grams and kilograms. A pound of product must be determined by weighing it in grams. The use of the term pound is usually forbidden for official trade purposes. Use in Commerce In the United States, the Department of Commerce, the Technology Administration, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have defined the use of mass and weight in the exchange of goods under the Uniform Laws and Regulations in the areas of legal metrology and engine fuel quality, as outlined in NIST Handbook 130. Federal law, which supersedes this handbook, also defines weight, particularly net weight, in terms of the avoirdupois pound or mass pound. This is specified in Section 51, Declaration of net quantity of contents, for general labeling and prescription labeling requirements.
